text: Multiple things can be true at the same time. The men accused in the Cornell case are entitled to due process. The woman who reported sexual assault deserves to be heard, treated with dignity and taken seriously. Women are scared at parties in parking lots and elevators. Men are angry about being stereotyped. All of those things can be true. But let's be brutally clear. Rape in any context is wrong. First, let's start with the breaking news in the Cornell case. On October 1st, Governor Carrie Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James's office to take over this case. Hochul said the new information had undermined her faith in the local district attorney's handling of it. That is a criticism of the investigation, not a finding that the accused are guilty. The executive order gives the Attorney General authority to investigate and, if warranted, prosecute and present evidence to a grand jury. The DA has been displaced in this case. He hasn't been removed from his elected office. So the questions were left open. First, why does the lawsuit describe events differently? We cannot fully resolve that yet. But remember, we were comparing the lawsuit with the DA's selected summary, not the complete police record. ABC's reporting shows that the signed statement already contained descriptions of coercion and inability to make decisions that his summary omitted. Some of the apparent gap, therefore, may come from what he selected. That is my reading of the situation, not a proven explanation for every difference. That doesn't explain every discrepancy, though. The DA's summary says she agreed to the first threesome. The lawsuit says she was already too intoxicated to consent. The summary describes the final encounter ending when she said she was tired and both men stopped as far as she remembered. The lawsuit says the alleged assault concluded around 5.45 a.m. and she lost consciousness. Even the wording differs. For example, the DA's summary says she and the third man began making out. The lawsuit says he began kissing her. By the way, in part one, I mistakenly used the lawsuit's wording when describing this part of DA's summary. Also, Jane Doe's lawyer says trauma affected how she understood and described the night. That is his explanation, not an established answer. Next, what did Cornell's investigation establish? According to Cornell's president, two of the seven were expelled, two were suspended for at least two semesters, one had already graduated, and two were found not responsible for sexual misconduct. These are university outcomes, not criminal verdicts. So the claim that two were expelled and everyone else just wrote essays repeated by Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez does not match that breakdown. The lawsuit says some could mitigate their conduct through essays. Cornell says essays were nobody's sole consequence. Whether its response was adequate remains a separate question. But how could Cornell find students responsible while the DA initially declined criminal charges? They applied different definitions and standards of proof. Cornell's definition of incapacity is broader and the university uses more likely than not, while a criminal conviction requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Under Cornell's policy, you are incapacitated if you can't knowingly choose to participate, whether your intoxication was voluntary or not. New York criminal law defines these categories more narrowly. Mental incapacitation involves being unable to appraise or control your conduct because of a substance administered without consent or another nonconsensual act. Physical helplessness means being unconscious or physically unable to communicate unwillingness. The DA concluded that her original statement established neither. ABC obtained a heavily redacted 99-page report from Cornell's own investigation into whether students violated its sexual misconduct policies. The university disciplinary process included 50 interviews with 32 witnesses, including accused fraternity members. But the findings differed between individuals, so we should not treat every disciplinary finding as a finding of SA. Now, why is the case back in the headlines nearly two years later? Partly because the lawsuit went viral in September and the pressure built from there. After it was filed in mid-September, the group chat screenshots spread. Florence Pugh and Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez spoke out. On September 28th, the DA reopened the case. And the next day, Governor Hoku called for an independent review. Also, what happened between campus police and the prosecutor? ABC reported that the DA said the group chat screenshot had never been provided to his office. Cornell says it sent it in November 2024. But the Associated Press also quoted him acknowledging receipt, leaving the timing unclear. DA said he never saw the transcript, while Cornell won't say whether it was included. And the DA didn't investigate independently. There's also a dispute about follow-up. The DA says he offered to meet Jane Doe through campus police, and that neither she nor her lawyers contacted his office in nearly two years. Her lawyer says nobody trained in interviewing survivors ever followed up with her. In any way, the DA reopened the case on September 28th. Subsequent reporting raised further questions about the original decision and the evidence he received. The important distinction is that the alleged incident happened in 2024. What is new is the lawsuit, public access to more of the records, and renewed scrutiny of how the case was handled. Now there are two separate processes, the Attorney General's criminal investigation and the outside review Cornell agreed to of its own response. Accused men who have responded through lawyers deny the allegations. The Attorney General will investigate and, if warranted, prosecute. My position hasn't changed since Part 1. This should be investigated thoroughly, and anyone proven guilty should face the full consequences of the law. But the way to get there is the evidence, and the new investigation needs to establish whether it supports criminal charges.
